title: Counting the cost of teaching higher education in England
summary: Last seen around the time of the Augar review, KPMG has updated work on the costs of teaching. DK finds evidence of cost cutting everywhere
full_text:
How much does it cost to teach an undergraduate student in England for a year, full time?

A new publication written by KPMG on behalf of the Department for Education – Understanding the cost of undergraduate provision and qualifications in the higher education sector in England – provides the latest answer to this perennial question, and the answer varies by subject area and provider.

Medicine, dentistry and veterinary sciences is the subject group with the highest cost – a cool £19,986 for a year of tuition. It is followed by physical sciences (£16,466), and an unlikely melange of earth sciences (geography, earth and environmental sciences, agriculture, food studies at £14,083).

Based on this data the least expensive subject areas are law (£9,475), combined and general studies (£10,276) and other social sciences (£10,340). Those familiar with TRAC data will note that all of these costs are higher than the maximum fee limit: the overall weighted average unit cost across all subjects is £12,317.

There is also a difference in costs between types of provider (and other factors that we will get to), this chart shows average costs for a year of undergraduate study split by subject and TRAC peer group (for the uninitiated, A and B are Russell Group and people who are nearly Russell group, D and E are generally smaller teaching focused universities, and C is the (squeezed) middle.

[Full screen]

A bit of context

The sticker price to the UK domiciled student (well, graduate technically) is £9,790: the same across all subjects and all Approved (Fee Cap) registered providers. How much the state actually pays out is modulated by the Office for Students’ use of the strategic priorities grant (SPG) – in particular a student premium that recognises the additional support required for non-traditional students, and a high cost subject supplement.

The cost of the latter was historically determined by an indicator known as Subject FACTs (the “Full Average subject-related Cost of Teaching and OfS-fundable FTE student in a cost centre” if you need that acronym for some reason). This used data collected within the TRAC(T) process to determine an average cost for each major subject area – more expensive subjects received a subsidy.

TRAC(T) data hasn’t been collected since 2019-20 – so the subject price groups OfS uses to allocate high cost supplements is getting on for seven years old. Even before then, it was seen as being past its best (there was a DfE review of TRAC(T) published alongside the Augar review back in May 2019)

What we have in this new report isn’t quite the subject FACTs approach – not least because it looks across just 29 universities and 9 FE colleges rather than the whole sector – but it represents valuable information for anyone trying to figure out what a high cost subject might be in 2026. In essence it looks a little bit like a smaller scale version of the KPMG work that underpinned the mysterious and arbitrary decision by Philip Augar and his panel to recommend that tuition fees should be £7,500.

A bit more on the methods

The figures I’ve cited above used 2023–24 TRAC data as a starting point (the college financial forecast return for the FE colleges), and this has been refined by multiple interactions and data collections with the providers involved. As such, it relies at least in part on providers’ own definitions of what is and isn’t a teaching cost (though this is mediated by TRACT definitions) and it doesn’t quite have the same status as the audited data we are used to in stuff like HESA Finance.

One advantage here is that when we talk about subject costs we are using HeCOS (as with teaching data) rather than cost centres (as with staff and finance data). This makes it easier to check up on student numbers in subjects, which makes the costs per student a little more robust.

It’s only a small sample but it is reasonably robust in terms of subject coverage and provider types for universities, though there is a slight bias towards the south of England and away from smaller providers. We’re only looking at six per cent of FE colleges that deliver HE – it is handy to have this information, but we need to be very careful in relying on it to make comparisons between FE and HE costs.

Expensive specialised equipment

We’re in the world of indicative data even before we started to think about coverage – the CAH1 subject groupings we are using contain a wide range of subjects and courses, all of which will likely have different costs. While the report can safely speculate that:

Specialist and technical courses often necessitate teaching staff with highly specific expertise… the delivery of these courses may demand bespoke physical infrastructure… technical and practical disciplines rely heavily on expensive, specialised equipment

and note that all of these aspects are going to add cost, it is important to note that we do mean “course” here and not “subject.” Film studies, for instance, is not going to have the same costs as film production.

Even within these broad subject areas we see institutional variation within our sample, which reflects – for many disciplines – huge variations in curriculum design and delivery. These differences are more visible in higher cost subjects than lower cost activity, although some of these differences (that we could ascribe to market-driven differentiation) are evened out by threshold professional body requirements.

What is interesting is that, while costs are higher than found in the 2019 study, they are not as high as the 2019 cost plus inflation (we are using RPIX here, which is what we persist in using in setting student loan interest rates). We are seeing very visible evidence of the cost savings that have seen staff cuts, low pay, and course closures in recent years – staff costs have risen by just 14 per cent compared to a 41.2 per cent cumulative RPIX since 2019, something that I am sure UCU is already printing on placards.

[Full screen]

Driving differences

Teaching at research-intensive providers is more expensive than teaching elsewhere; likewise delivery using a lower student/staff ratio costs more. As above, specialist courses have their own expensive requirements. And it’s 12 per cent more expensive to do pretty much anything in London.

All of these factors play a part in our understanding of cost variations across subject areas too: a specialist subject (for example medicine) delivered primarily by research-intensive providers in small classes will look more expensive even before we start thinking about what makes medicine different from nursing.

A few other factors are slightly more surprising – foundation degrees, your archetypal sub-degree qualification, looks more expensive per year than traditional undergraduate degrees. As – sorry DfE – do foundation years. We are dealing here with very low numbers of students within the sample, to be clear.

And – expect a lot of hay to be made about this – the average cost of a year of degree tuition in an FE college is just £6,287. As well as the other factors noted above (subject mix, non-specialist provision, variations in staffing type and level) we need to be aware that this represents a tiny non-representative sample of FE colleges.

One thing that is in here but will not be driving differences is the margin for sustainability and investment (MSI – which is set for 2023-24 at a blanket 9 per cent). For some reason the idea that universities may have historic losses to recoup, and solid risk mitigation policies that require some funding to be held to cover known future costs, was very controversial around the time of Augar. Calculated based on audited financial statements and projections, this calculation was last reviewed in 2025, and the updated figures are represented in this years’ TRAC.

Policy implications

This exercise sets out clearly that, in the overwhelming majority of cases, the cost of teaching in a university is not covered by the tuition fee. It also demonstrates that the savings that providers have made in order to address this gap have hit academic staff particularly hard – but mean that, in real terms, university teaching is cheaper now than it was in 2019.

For anyone who works in a university neither of these things will be unexpected. Neither will the fact that, due to recruitment pressures, some universities are currently carrying higher costs per FTE student than were planned or budgeted for.

The addition of a very limited analysis of HE teaching within FE colleges poses more questions than it answers – it is not a safe conclusion to decide that FE colleges are doing a comparable activity cheaper. If this is an argument DfE wishes to make, it needs to collect a lot more data. Likewise, we have very limited data on costs within specialist providers, or on the costs of part time or online (or even blended approaches).

It’s an open secret that OfS and DfE are both thinking very carefully about the future allocation of the strategic priorities grant – should it be used to prop up high-cost courses where student demand exists that would otherwise be unviable, or should it be used to shape the sector via strategic allocations linked to government priorities?

This is not a straightforward question for either body to answer. But the sector is shrinking (unless we see a far more radical policy and funding settlement than pretty much anyone is expecting in the coming budget) – and a managed decline is preferable to a series of disorderly market exits. The decision ministers need to make is about what to save and what to let go. And I don’t envy them that.

title: We are paying a high price for a university education | Letters
summary:
Readers respond to an article by Zoe Williams in which she argues that university has become a scam

Having read Zoe Williams’ article on student loans (Why has university become such a scam?, 14 September), I went and checked my student loan statement. What a depressing read that was. I went to university in 2012 as a slightly older student, at 22. I had been to drama school before that, but decided I wasn’t cut out for the harsh reality of show business and that a law career – a barrister perhaps – was more up my street. I wanted to keep the performance element.

After one law degree totalling £56,000, a career development loan of £15,000 to cover the cost of my bar course and a £12,000 postgraduate loan to cover my legal practice course (solicitor training), my student debt remains at £70,000.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Having read Zoe Williams’ article on student loans (Why has university become such a scam?, 14 September), I went and checked my student loan statement. What a depressing read that was. I went to university in 2012 as a slightly older student, at 22. I had been to drama school before that, but decided I wasn’t cut out for the harsh reality of show business and that a law career – a barrister perhaps – was more up my street. I wanted to keep the performance element.

After one law degree totalling £56,000, a career development loan of £15,000 to cover the cost of my bar course and a £12,000 postgraduate loan to cover my legal practice course (solicitor training), my student debt remains at £70,000.

I am now a solicitor for the NHS, working four days a week to manage childcare costs. The £150 in loan repayments out of my salary each month mean very little when £1,500 is added in interest each year. That £150 could instead be going into the pocket of my landlord as he hikes the rent again or towards the high private nursery fees for my son so that I can go to work. When his time comes to consider higher education, I will very much be encouraging an alternative route.

Nerys Cookson-Williams

Llandogo, Monmouthshire

As the mother of a new undergraduate, the student loans farce makes me livid. With about £24bn paid out yearly and only around £5bn returned in repayments, it will never pay for itself, so why put young people through this horrific system?

More importantly, it’s working-class and middle-class young people who are affected by what has effectively become another tax – as the rich don’t need loans, they aren’t affected by it. Until this is sorted, universities will once again become inaccessible to the majority of young people. Surely free university education for all is the way forward, alongside a fresh focus on vocational training?

Emily Miller

Mildenhall, Suffolk

Zoe Williams is right to highlight the scandal of student debt. However, it is even more sinister when you consider the free labour propping up the NHS. Last month, after three thankless years, I finished my final 12.5-hour night shift as a student midwife. Having worked tirelessly for over 2,300 unpaid hours, I am graduating into unemployment with a £50,000 debt and a heavy heart.

Universities continue to host large cohorts of midwifery students, each paying £9,750 per year for the privilege, despite the crisis in recruitment. NHS trusts are paid to host students who work gruelling hours for no pay. This is nothing short of exploitation.

Zoe Green

London

I wholly agree that students are being done a huge disservice. But as an employer, I disagree with casually blaming employers for the drop in graduate jobs. First, the economy is in the doldrums and the cost of employment has risen. With low growth the default, when national insurance goes up it directly hits our margins and reduces the amount of new starters we can afford to take on or pay rises we can afford.

The courses that students pay a fortune for are also a problem. As a digital marketing employer, digital marketing degrees are not desirable. An education system that delivers more capable staff, or incentivises employers to provide them with meaningful training, would do wonders for graduate recruitment.

Name and address supplied

With regard to the unfairness heaped on today’s graduates, there is a simple answer out there – a (smaller) graduate tax on all graduates. If all graduates are asked to share the burden, the marginal tax rate could fall to 3% or 4%. Most, if not all, those currently paying student loans would favour it (with the option of staying on the current plan to anyone who has repaid in full or is about to), and it would be likely to appeal to many older graduates with children or grandchildren caught up in the current system.

Anyone who says this is impractical because there is no list of all graduates is being disingenuous. The Student Loans Company has lists of all graduates since 1998; a tick box on self-assessment forms would cover millions more, and asking employees to self-declare via their employer’s PAYE scheme would do likewise. Sufficient penalty deterrents could mop up most of the remainder. Given current funding solutions for higher education are generally considered a mess by all interested parties, I’m surprised that this hasn’t been given wider consideration.

Alan Terry

Exeter

Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please emailus your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Many HBCUs Thrive as Other Institutions Struggle to Enroll Enough Students
summary:
Many HBCUs Thrive as Other Institutions Struggle to Enroll Enough Students Olivia.sanchez Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM The enrollment growth has been accompanied by growing pains, leaders say, as they figure out how to house, feed and teach more students. Byline(s) Olivia Sanchez Many HBCUs Thrive as Other Institutions Struggle to Enroll Enough Students
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

The enrollment growth has been accompanied by growing pains, leaders say, as they figure out how to house, feed and teach more students.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Concerns about enrollment plague college leaders across the country, who fear what will happen to their institutions as fewer 18-year-olds graduate from high school and fading faith in higher education deters others. But even as many predominantly white, regional and private colleges struggle to fill seats, some historically Black colleges and universities are seeing heightened—in some cases record—interest, applications and enrollment.

As one expert put it, the increased interest in HBCUs can be explained by a long-standing message on a digital billboard on a Baltimore campus: “Morgan State University, where Black lives have always mattered.”

Across the country, 42 of 101 HBCUs grew their enrollment between 2019 and 2024, according to federal data. Many increased head count significantly in that period: Howard University grew by 50 percent, Morgan State by 42 percent, Virginia State University by 27 percent and Elizabeth City State University by 23 percent. Since then, enrollment has continued to climb, according to several colleges that provided enrollment figures to Inside Higher Ed. (Some predominantly white institutions have also seen unexpected enrollment gains.)

Not all HBCUs have been so lucky. A few have maintained relatively stable enrollment, while others faced major enrollment declines and, in the case of St. Augustine’s University in North Carolina, serious financial trouble and bankruptcy.

But among those seeing an upswing, experts said a combination of factors is driving the interest. For one thing, students are growing more aware of HBCUs—thanks to high-profile HBCU alumni such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and the ever-growing use of social media to document campus life. At the same time, students may be deterred from predominantly white institutions for a number of reasons, including acts of racist violence like the 2020 murder of George Floyd, the Supreme Court’s ban on the consideration of race in admissions and the Trump administration’s campaign against all things diversity, equity and inclusion.

“Seeing this on display really calls us to understand what we call ‘home’ and where we are thriving—in environments that were created for us and that are foundational to our identities,” said Leslie U. Ekpe, a professor of higher education at East Texas A&M University. “We talk about belonging in higher education and how critical it is to one’s well-being and success, and I think HBCUs have paved the way to show that Black students are welcome, they’re celebrated.”

Ekpe, who researches minority-serving institutions, said heightened interest in HBCUs serves as a reminder that “we should have never been looking at HBCUs through a deficit lens.”

More Students, More Challenges

But more students means more pressure on HBCUs to accommodate them. Jorge Burmicky, a professor of higher education leadership and policy studies at Howard University, said that as enrollment grows, HBCU leaders must consider the demand on faculty and staff to meet students’ needs.

Students need to be connected with advising and tutoring, gain entry to required classes, get help from financial aid officers when necessary, and access mental health services in a timely manner, Burmicky said. As part of a separate research project, Burmicky recently interviewed faculty and staff from six HBCUs, many of whom reported struggling to meet student demand as enrollment at their institutions grew.

“It’s fine for us to celebrate growing enrollment—for a lot of HBCUs that’s been a blessing. But equally as important is making sure that we are investing in the capacity so that we’re not so stretched thin," Burmicky said. “Because the reality is that it doesn’t just hurt faculty and staff, it also hurts the student experience.”

Kara Turner, senior vice president of enrollment management and student success at Morgan State, said the university’s enrollment growth can be attributed not just to the growing interest in HBCUs in general, but also to her institution’s concerted recruiting effort.

During the pandemic, university officials realized they could reach more students using virtual recruitment sessions and campus tours, she said. Eventually they hired a recruiter based in the Midwest to expand the university’s geographical reach.

The effort paid off: Enrollment exploded from 7,151 students in 2019 to 12,477 in 2026. But that rapid growth has created new challenges.

In the last few years, the university has built three new residence halls (two of which are open now) and remodeled several others. To fill the gaps, the university leased units from nearby apartment complexes so that students could still get their housing through Morgan; others are being temporarily housed in hotels until the new residence halls open, Turner said.

“Of course there are growing pains when you grow and you grow fast. But the university has been nimble,” Turner said. “We wanted the students. The students were interested and we wanted them and so we said, ‘All right, we’re going to figure this out.’”

North Carolina A&T University, which grew from 13,300 students in 2021 to 15,713 this fall, also put students up in hotels as a new residence hall was under construction.

Beyond housing, university leaders have had to consider how their swelling student body can get their financial aid and register for classes on time, said Dawn M. Nail, the university’s interim associate vice provost for enrollment management. The university moved the treasurer, registrar and financial aid offices into one building to make the process more efficient.

The pressure on HBCUs has manifested in different ways. Howard University disenrolled 502 students over the summer and then re-enrolled about 200, after officials said the students hadn’t met their payment deadline. Keyana Scales, Howard University’s senior vice president for enrollment management, told WJLA News 7 that it was a matter of reduced resources. A spokesperson from Howard declined to answer questions about enrollment growth for this article.

At some HBCUs, the enrollment figures do not necessarily reflect the extent of their increased popularity. For example, Spelman College in Atlanta has seen such a rise in applications that the admissions rate went from 51 percent to 19 percent in the last five years, largely because leaders have chosen to keep enrollment relatively stable.

“There’s a real energy to it. A more geographically diverse and competitive applicant pool means more perspectives in the classroom, even as we stay intentional about our size,” Chelsea Holley, Spelman’s director of admissions, said in an email.

Holley said the college is building two residence halls because they want to accommodate all the Spelman undergraduates who choose to live on campus for all four years.

“Our goal isn’t to become huge,” Holley said. “We’re a small liberal arts college, and we want to expand the resources that support students throughout their time here, not the number of seats.”

title: When Basic Needs Go on Credit
summary:
When Basic Needs Go on Credit Joshua.Bay Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM New Trellis Strategies research finds students with unpaid credit card balances experience greater financial strain and difficulty concentrating on schoolwork. Byline(s) Joshua Bay When Basic Needs Go on Credit
Joshua.Bay Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

New Trellis Strategies research finds students with unpaid credit card balances experience greater financial strain and difficulty concentrating on schoolwork.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
For some college students, covering basic needs means taking on debt. Some put expenses such as food, housing and transportation on credit cards, and many carry unpaid balances as they manage the costs of college. New research from Trellis Strategies suggests that financial strain can follow students into the classroom, making it more difficult to focus on their studies.

The data comes from the postsecondary research and consulting firm’s 2025 Student Financial Wellness Survey, which drew more than 65,000 responses from undergraduates at 153 institutions in 23 states, including over 32,000 credit card users. It found that 54 percent of respondents reported using a credit card in 2025, up from 43 percent in 2018.

Fewer than half of student cardholders (47 percent) pay their balance in full each month, the survey showed. Among those carrying a balance, 88 percent said they worried about covering basic monthly expenses, compared with 61 percent of those who pay in full. Some 60 percent of students carrying unpaid balances also reported difficulty concentrating on schoolwork due to financial stress, compared with 43 percent of those who pay their balances in full.

Bryan Ashton, managing director at Trellis Strategies and co-author of the report, said the findings highlight the financial pressures students can face as the cost of living rises while their options for borrowing to cover expenses outside of tuition remain limited.

“We have limitations on what we can do with student loans, especially federal student loans, because of caps,” Ashton said. “But when indirect costs go up—cost of living, housing, food, transportation—we don’t really see the ability for students to increase borrowing without going to the private market. So sometimes credit cards become the one way that students can close that indirect-cost gap.”

Basic needs on credit: The report found that 88 percent of student cardholders reported using credit cards for basic needs such as food, housing and transportation.

While 75 percent of student cardholders reported paying their credit card bills on time, 14 percent said they struggled to do so. Among students who do not pay their balances in full each month, that share rises to 31 percent.

Ashton said using a credit card to pay for basic needs is not necessarily a problem. The bigger concern is what happens when students cannot pay off those expenses and begin carrying revolving debt from month to month.

“The bigger challenge is the number that are not then able to pay off that expense,” Ashton said. “As you get into these revolving credit situations, one of the concerns that we have is ‘What is the credit limit attached to these? When will we run out of that opportunity?’ And then, secondarily, the higher [annual percentage rate] that students are paying to finance those expenses during that period of time.”

Alexandra Penrose, research analyst at Trellis Strategies and co-author of the report, said financial pressures do not remain separate from students’ academic lives.

“When we struggle to fully pay off things in life, it then automatically bleeds into our academic work and studies,” Penrose said. “It’s really hard to separate financial pressures from what students are doing in school.”

Among students using credit cards for basic needs, 58 percent expressed concern about their ability to cover monthly expenses, and roughly one-third said their overall debt felt unmanageable.

As interest accumulates on unpaid credit card balances, Ashton said, students can find themselves increasingly struggling to catch up, which can take a mental toll.

“We see that with credit card utilization, too, because that interest compounds so quickly that the inability to catch up can drive some of the anxiety and depression we see in students.”

Addressing financial strain: The report notes that helping students better understand how consumer credit works, including responsible use and repayment expectations, can reduce the risk of debt accumulating to unmanageable levels.

Ashton noted that institutions often allow students to pay tuition with credit cards. While that can be a routine way for some students to finance their education, he said credit card payments can also signal financial strain. Institutions could provide students with information about credit and repayment when they choose to pay tuition by card, he said.

Colleges can also help students reduce their reliance on credit cards for basic needs by connecting them with public benefits that can offset the costs of food, housing and other necessities, he added.

“Continuing to educate on the role of interest and what it means to use credit is important and something that we’ve gotten away from on campuses over the last couple decades,” Ashton said.

Penrose said institutions can offer lower-cost alternatives to credit cards, including payment plans, while also embedding financial education into courses to help students understand how to manage their expenses.

“When students use these high-interest credit card options to pay for their educational expenses, it should be a signal for institutions that there is a need that needs to be addressed for students to successfully go through college,” Penrose said.

title: Legacy Preferences Have Declined but Persist at Highly Selective Colleges
summary:
Legacy Preferences Have Declined but Persist at Highly Selective Colleges Johanna Alonso Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM Byline(s) Johanna Alonso Legacy Preferences Have Declined but Persist at Highly Selective Colleges
Johanna Alonso Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
The number of institutions that give applicants a boost if their parents graduated from the same college or university has declined significantly in the past decade, according to a new report by Class Action, an advocacy and research organization that critiques elitism in higher education.

Legacy preferences have dipped across almost all types of institutions, writes the report’s author, senior fellow James Murphy—except for wealthy, highly selective private institutions.

Of the more than 1,700 four-year institutions Murphy analyzed, about half considered a student’s legacy status in their admissions processes as of 2015. But in 2024, the most recent year for which data was available, only 23 percent continued to do so, a decline of more than half. When counting all the institutions of higher education in the country, including community colleges, that number drops to just 7 percent.

But the more selective a college is, Murphy writes, the more likely it is to consider legacy status. Among the 89 institutions that admit 25 percent of applicants or fewer, 57 percent had legacy preferences in 2024. For those with acceptance rates between 26 and 50 percent, 33 percent considered legacy. Among those with acceptance rates between 51 and 75 percent, 27 percent considered legacy.

On the other hand, such preferences are rare at public colleges. In half of states, no public colleges utilize legacy in admissions.

Murphy writes that legacy admissions likely persist at highly selective institutions because “too many elites look at their privileges as their rights,” even as the majority of Americans agree such preferences are unfair. He notes that some institutions appear to be making an effort to conceal their use of legacy status as the practice becomes less popular; some institutions that previously publicized the percentage of their incoming classes that were legacy now no longer do so.

“At a moment when the wealthiest colleges and universities are somewhat unjustly being accused of being out of step with normal American values, their continued use of legacy preferences makes it clear that the accusations are not completely off base,” the report’s conclusion states. “Eliminating legacy preferences will not fix all that is wrong in college admissions, let alone higher education, but it would send a clear sign that elite institutions understand what normal people believe are the rules of fair play and want to play by them, too. Unfortunately, this is not a signal that many of these institutions want to send.”

title: The Education Department’s Push for Accreditation Reform Could Backfire
summary:
The Education Department’s Push for Accreditation Reform Could Backfire sara.custer@in… Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM An agency leader says the proposed rules could disrupt the balance of power and stifle innovation. Byline(s) Sara Custer The Education Department’s Push for Accreditation Reform Could Backfire
sara.custer@in… Thu, 09/17/2026 - 03:00 AM

An agency leader says the proposed rules could disrupt the balance of power and stifle innovation.

Byline(s)
Sara Custer
full_text:
In an interview for Inside Higher Ed’s podcast The Key, I asked Maria Toyoda, CEO of the WASC Senior College and University Commission, which part of the Education Department’s proposed changes to accreditation would be most disruptive. I didn’t get the straightforward answer I expected. She didn’t say, for example, policing research integrity or the end of peer review. Instead, Toyoda responded with how the 80 pages of proposed rules, published last month, could change the very nature of accreditation in this country—and perhaps not in the way the department would like.

The Higher Education Act, first passed in 1965, lays out the three-part system of higher ed oversight: the federal government, state agencies and accreditors, she told me. The government and accreditors have clear, independent roles. Toyoda described it as a dichotomy baked into the law itself. “You’ve got substance and you’ve got process,” she said. “And where the federal government lands is, they can tell us about what should be in our processes.” Under the law, the government can regulate whether accreditors have standards and how they’re applied, but not what those standards are. Yet, “What you’re seeing in [the new rules] is it looks like something that they are prescribing us to do,” Toyoda said. “They are then coming right up to that line that could be crossed from being a process to being something of substance.”

One place she thinks that line could be crossed? The proposed protections for academic freedom and the First Amendment. The proposal doesn’t go as far as defining academic freedom, but the department says accrediting agencies would need to evaluate if any institutional policies protect civil rights and First Amendment rights, and whether those policies include academic freedom protections “that are clearly articulated and applied consistently to faculty regardless of appointment classification, race or other immutable characteristics, viewpoint, or ideology.” The department also said it would like agencies to “require” that an institution’s policies include freedom-of-inquiry protections.

Currently, “All of us review things like academic freedom,” Toyoda said of accrediting bodies. But “we’re not telling institutions what their academic freedom policies are. We’re asking them, do you have a policy and are you following that policy and are you following it consistently? We’re not prescribing to them what that language must say.”

Not only does the department’s overhaul potentially violate the Higher Education Act, “there could be a very significant shift in terms of this relationship that institutions have with their accreditors,” Toyoda said.

Going further, she argued that requiring accreditors to apply rigid rules to all institutions is not only unrealistic—it could stifle innovation. “None of us, I think, disagree with that basic philosophy around accountability,” she said. “The thing is that you can never write a rule that prescribes exactly how you’re going to get from point A to point B without it applying uniformly to all kinds of institutions.” For example, assessing a small private liberal arts institution by the same rule as a large public research university is “impractical” and “undermines what I would view as the genius of higher education in the U.S., which is to try different things,” she said.

But supporting innovation is exactly what the department says these new regulations are meant to do. Cutting red tape around new accreditor recognition is part of that goal. Education Under Secretary Nicholas Kent has said that with more accreditors, the market will be more dynamic and agencies would be incentivized to differentiate themselves. Toyoda said she agrees that more institutional accreditors will bring healthy competition, but she questions that logic for programmatic accreditors, who could “water down” their standards.

Toyoda isn’t the only one who agrees, at least in theory, that competition is a good thing. In its public comment on the proposed rules, the Middle States Commission on Higher Education also supported more competition and easing the process to switch accreditors. But it encouraged the department to ensure the rules provide an appropriate level of flexibility for accreditors and their practices. “We celebrate that institutions have choices when it comes to accreditation; however, accreditors must also be permitted to have different policies and procedures that make us uniquely attractive to institutions,” MSCHE President Heather Perfetti wrote.

Toyoda is less certain that institutions will accreditor-hop the way the department hopes. The rules might streamline the process for switching, but colleges will be burdened by what comes after, she said.

“You have to learn all these new standards and you have to apply all these standards in the way that the accreditor is seeking to have you apply them. For most institutions, this means starting from scratch with a self-study that is written up against these new standards and the ways in which the new accreditor is seeking evidentiary guidance and all of that kind of stuff,” she said. “Switching itself is easy. It’s what comes after that’s going to be complicated for institutions.”

A July survey of more than 320 institutional leaders by the American Council on Education backs her up: Only 5 percent said their institution was likely to change agencies if the rules are adopted. And in Inside Higher Ed’s forthcoming annual survey of chief academic officers, out next week, just 17 percent predict the planned federal accreditation overhaul will have a somewhat or strongly positive impact on higher education.

Toyoda framed the department’s proposals within the context of the three-way balance of power in higher ed oversight. By being too prescriptive in its new regulations, the federal government risks encroaching on accreditors’ independence, which could undermine its aims. The government says it wants more innovation, more competition among accreditors and more intellectual diversity. But without sector support, it might not achieve any of those.

title: How the Federal Reserve's rate hike impacts student loan interest rates
full_text:
The Federal Reserve doesn't set student loan rates directly, but its federal funds rate influences the 10-year Treasury yield (which determines federal loan rates) and the prime rate (which determines private loan rates).

But exactly how the Fed affects your cost of borrowing depends on the type of student loans and interest rate you have.

After the Federal Reserve's September 2026 meeting, it raised interest rates by 25 basis points. See how that might impact the cost of your student loans.

How does the Federal Reserve influence student loan interest rates?

One of the Federal Reserve's main goals is to keep inflation under control. It does this partly by adjusting the federal funds rate — the rate banks charge one another for short-term loans.

When inflation rises above the Fed's 2% target, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) may raise the federal funds rate to cool the economy. That move typically pushes up the prime rate, which banks use to set interest rates on loans and credit cards. As borrowing becomes more expensive, consumers and businesses tend to spend less, which can help bring prices back down.

The reverse is also true. When inflation slows or the economy weakens, the Fed may lower rates to encourage borrowing and spending, which can stimulate growth.

In short, changes to the federal funds rate ripple through the economy — influencing everything from mortgage rates to credit cards — as the Fed tries to balance inflation and economic stability.

Federal student loans

The federal funds rate doesn't directly determine federal student loan interest rates, but it can influence them indirectly. Congress sets the federal student loan rates based on the 10-year Treasury note, adding a fixed margin each year.

But the 10-year Treasury yield moves with investor demand, not the Fed's rate. When investors expect high inflation or strong economic growth, they demand higher yields, which can push federal student loan rates higher.

That said, if the Fed's rate hikes successfully cool inflation, Treasury yields may drop — and the following year's federal student loan rates could be lower.

Key takeaway: Since federal student loans come with fixed interest rates, any change only affects new loans, not those you already have.

Private student loans

Private student loans are offered by banks, credit unions, and online lenders, many of which use the prime rate as a basis for setting their interest rates. The prime rate moves alongside the Federal Reserve's rate decisions. So, when the Fed raises rates, new private loan rates usually rise, and when it cuts rates, they tend to fall.

That said, how much this impacts you depends on your loan type. Fixed-rate loans lock in one rate for the life of the loan, so if you borrow when rates are high, you'll keep that rate even if they later drop. Variable-rate loans, on the other hand, fluctuate with the market, so your rate and your payment can go up or down over time with the prime rate.

Key takeaway: Borrowers with fixed-rate loans are unaffected, but those with variable rates will likely see their rates change with Federal Reserve decisions.

Interest rates for different types of student loans

Each year, Congress determines interest rates on federal student loans for the entire academic year by taking the 10-year Treasury rate on a specific date in May and adding a margin, which varies by loan type. For the 2026-27 school year, the 10-year Treasury note high yield was set at 4.468%, with the following margins:

These interest rates are standardized within each program. If you apply for financial aid with a Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) application and qualify for a federal student loan, you'll receive the same rate as everyone else who qualifies in the same year.

Private student loan rates

On the other hand, private lenders determine interest rates using the prime rate and other benchmarks as well as risk-based pricing.

Instead of offering a standardized rate, they typically offer a range of interest rates, with the best student loan rates reserved for the most creditworthy borrowers and higher rates for borrowers with a higher risk of defaulting on payments.

Among private lenders, interest rates can vary depending on the lender, your creditworthiness, and the type of interest rate you choose. That said, the typical fixed interest rate among top private student loan companies ranges from about 2% to 17% as of September 2026.

Read more: What is a good student loan interest rate?

Do credit scores and co-signers also affect your interest rate?

You don't need a minimum credit score or a co-signer to qualify for federal student loans. However, if you're applying for private student loans, a bad credit score will likely prevent you from qualifying — you typically need a credit score in the mid-600s or higher to get approved.

Just because you qualify doesn't mean you'll get favorable terms — student loan companies reserve their highest loan amounts and lowest rates for borrowers with credit scores in the mid-700s and higher.

If you can't qualify for a private student loan on your own, or you can't get a low interest rate, you can improve your odds by adding a creditworthy co-signer to your application. A co-signer agrees to repay the loan if you can't, so the lender will also consider their credit score and income during the application process.

If you don't have a potential co-signer, improving your credit score is your best bet to qualify for a lower rate on a private student loan. Steps you can take include:

Checking your credit score to evaluate your overall credit health

Reviewing your credit reports to pinpoint areas you can address

Paying your bills on time and, if applicable, getting caught up on missed payments

Paying down high credit card balances

Paying off loans with low balances

Asking a loved one with good credit to add you as an authorized user on their credit card

Disputing inaccurate or fraudulent information on your credit reports

Will refinancing your student loans lower your interest rate?

Student loan refinancing involves replacing your existing loans with a new one through a private lender. Depending on your situation, refinancing may allow you to secure a lower interest rate or a more favorable repayment plan. If you have several loans, you'll also be able to consolidate them into one monthly payment going forward.

If you have private student loans and can qualify for better terms with a refinance loan, there aren't many downsides to refinancing. But if you have federal student loans, it's important to consider what you'll give up if you refinance them with a private lender. The process is irreversible and will result in you losing access to federal benefits, including student loan forgiveness and repayment assistance programs, income-driven repayment plans, and generous forbearance and deferment options.

Unless you have a stable job and income and the potential savings are significant, it's best to avoid refinancing federal student loans.

The bottom line

Ultimately, while the Federal Reserve plays an indirect but powerful role in shaping student loan interest rates, what really matters is the type of loan you have and how you manage it. Federal loan borrowers can rest easy knowing their fixed rates won't change, but future students may see higher (or lower) rates depending on where inflation and Treasury yields move.

Private loan borrowers, on the other hand, will continue to feel the Fed's decisions more directly through changes to the prime rate, especially if they have variable-rate loans.

If you're looking to reduce the cost of your student loans, start by reviewing your current interest rates and comparing them with today's averages. Borrowers with strong credit and steady income may qualify for lower rates through refinancing, which can help save money over time.

You can estimate your potential savings with a student loan refinancing calculator, then check your pre-qualified offers from multiple lenders to see what's available — all without affecting your credit score. Taking the time to explore your options now can make repayment more manageable in the long run.

title: International student declines hit US college revenues, survey finds
summary:
Nearly three-quarters of US college leaders say international student declines are squeezing institutional revenues, as federal policy actions bite.

The post International student declines hit US college revenues, survey finds appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
A new report from the American Council on Education (ACE) has revealed international student declines are having a tangible fiscal impact on campuses across the US, with 73% of senior leaders reporting decreased revenues, and 59% citing extreme or moderate concern for immigration restrictions and visa revocations.

Public perceptions about the value of postsecondary education, and long-term financial viability were the most pressing issues cited by the 300 leaders across US institutions and systems.

“As the new academic year begins, postsecondary leaders are confronting a volatile environment shaped by public scepticism about the value of college, heightened federal and state policy intervention, and mounting institutional pressures around finances and enrolment,” wrote the survey authors, Ezequiel Jimenez and Danielle Melidona.

At the institutional level, nearly half of respondents (49%) indicated the long-term financial viability of their university was their most pressing concern, with two in 10 reporting extreme concern.

At the sector level, leaders displayed the most concern for policymaker and public perceptions of the value of postsecondary education.

Strikingly, over eight in 10 respondents reported extreme (54%) or moderate (28%) concern about how state and federal decision makers perceive higher education, while nearly three-quarters were worried about public perceptions of value.

Meanwhile, three quarters of presidents reported extreme or moderate concern for academic freedom and institutional autonomy, with this issue topping the list of matters for which senior leaders felt they were the least prepared to navigate.

It comes as US higher education is increasingly being questioned by those in power, illustrated by the myriad policy changes under the Trump administration hiking visa barriers for international students, challenging institutional autonomy and scrutinising links with international partners.

Postsecondary leaders are confronting a volatile environment shaped by public scepticism about the value of college

Ezequiel Jimenez & Danielle Melidona, ACE

Federal research funding has also come under pressure, with grants withheld from some institutions and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) dramatically slowing its funding of biomedical research.

Among presidents at four-year public institutions, 62% said funding reductions had decreased revenue, with more than one in three reporting a slowdown in research output.

What’s more, senior leaders highlighted concerns about restrictive conditions being attached to federal grants and increasing regulation that limits innovation.

As for those reporting international student declines, the functional consequences varied. While nearly a quarter reported budget reductions in research or student support, 9% said programs had closed or merged, and 11% reported a decrease in financial aid.

Across the board, 85% of presidents said the current policy environment had affected their ability to deliver financial aid. The survey also asked leaders about accreditation challenges and their preparedness to comply with new federal reporting requirements associated with Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB).

Elsewhere, among leaders’ written answers, artificial intelligence emerged as a cross-cutting concern, with the report warning that AI had “reached a threshold of urgency”.

title: The hidden cost of outdated content on university websites
summary: Outdated web content does more than create untidy pages. It can erode student trust, weaken recruitment journeys, increase compliance risk, waste staff time, and make institutional websites harder to manage. What's the cost of content decay, and what can you do about it?
full_text:
An outdated page on your university or college website rarely announces itself.

It may still look polished, load quickly, and sit comfortably within your latest higher ed design; but maybe it's got a deadline from the previous year, or the tuition fees haven't been updated, or even lists a scholarship that doesn't exist anymore, or a professor who's retired.

One page can seem harmless, but across a large higher education website, those pages can start to add up…

…And so do the consequences, because the real risk isn't just having an "untidy" website.

Outdated content can cause friction around recruitment, give a student the wrong information at critical touchpoints like applications, and maybe even send that student right back to Google looking for an answer they trust more.

It can weaken trust, disrupt your student recruitment journeys, create compliance risks, and generate extra work across your institution.

When we talk to clients about this, we describe it as content debt: easy to ignore at first, increasingly expensive the longer it builds up.

Outdated content can become a bigger risk

Yeah sure, an outdated campus news story could be mildly embarrassing, but outdated or incorrect tuition fees, application deadlines, entry requirements, or course descriptions are a different matter.

Students use this information to decide where to study, what they can afford and whether a course is right for them.

So imagine your current course page says one fee, while an older PDF that's still available from a Google Search (and our Gen Z do love to search!) says another. Or a programme page describes modules that are no longer offered.

That's not just a content-maintenance problem.

At best, it creates confusion and extra inquiries… at worst, that inaccurate or misleading information can lead to complaints, requests for redress, regulatory scrutiny, or legal issues.

And there's a reputational risk sitting alongside the compliance one.

If a prospective student has to email your university to ask which of two published tuition fees is correct, confidence in the rest of the information on your website can disappear pretty quickly.

Then there's the less visible cost: the admissions queries, corrections, duplicated effort and extra work when your next redesign or migration rolls around.

We tend to think of this as content debt. It's rarely caused by one disastrous page; it builds gradually, as content is published, copied, forgotten and left behind.

Outdated doesn't just mean old

A university history page published in 2019 may still be completely accurate, while course page updated yesterday could contain a fee copied from an outdated document.

So age alone isn't particularly useful when you're trying to limit outdated content: what matters more is whether somebody can still rely on the information today.

And, quite often, when there's outdated content, it's because no one is really too sure who owns the original page anymore.

When small inaccuracies become a trust problem

Imagine you're researching where to study and find three different tuition fees across the same university website.

You're probably not thinking about publishing workflows or how responsibilities are divided between faculties and the central web team. You just want to know which figure is right.

Prospective students can arrive almost anywhere on your website through search (and they do love to search), social media, AI answer engines, old emails and bookmarked links.

A forgotten PDF several levels down can still become somebody's first impression of your institution.

We've written before about higher ed journeys becoming trust journeys, and content accuracy is a fairly fundamental part of that.

Your website is often where people go to confirm something they've seen elsewhere, but finding three different answers doesn't exactly help.

There's a recruitment cost, too

Perhaps a prospective student follows a link to a program that isn't offered anymore. Or they find an old campus tour registration page through search.

Or worse, they plan their application using last year's deadline because it's listed on an old page.

None of these is a dramatic website failure; in fact, technically, the website may be working perfectly.

But now the visitor has another job: work out which information is correct.

They might keep searching, they might email admissions…or they might head back to Google and find another college or university that makes the answer easier to find.

From our point of view, this is an important part of UX too: a website can be beautifully designed and easy to navigate, but if the content itself can't be trusted, the experience still breaks down.

Start with the content where mistakes matter

If your university or college website contains tens of thousands of pages, you're hardly going to "review everything."

Instead, we'd start with the areas where getting something wrong could genuinely affect a student decision:

course and programme information

tuiton fees

entry requirements

application deadlines

scholarships

accommodation

visa information

and important student support information.

Your old university news page from 2017 can probably wait, but the wrong application deadline can't.

This makes a content review a much less daunting. task.Instead of treating every page as equally urgent, you can focus time and attention where it has the most value.

Who owns what?

Content ownership is often where things get a bit murky sometimes.

Your web team might publish a course page, but they probably aren't the people who decide the fee.

Admissions may know the deadline, but a faculty member may own the programme information, and somebody else manages scholarships.

That's fine. Content ownership doesn't mean one person has to know everything.

But it does help if there's somebody responsible for making sure the right people are asked.

For important content, it's worth knowing who owns the page, who can verify the information, and when it was last properly reviewed.

It's also worth thinking about what happens when that person changes role or leaves. In our experience, this one catches more websites out than you might expect.

Give different content different lifespans

There's no particular reason to review an evergreen campus history page as often as application deadlines.

Fees, deadlines, entry requirements and application instructions may need checking several times during a recruitment cycle.

Course information, accommodation and support services might be reviewed annually.

Other pages are better linked to an event: a member of staff leaves, a policy changes, a course closes or a campaign ends.

And a review doesn't necessarily mean rewriting anything, it could just be as simple as showing it to the right person who can confirm the info's still valid.

So, how do you actually find outdated content?

On a large university or college website, you probably already know there's outdated content somewhere. You know there is!

The harder question is where to start looking.

Begin with a few obvious signals

Look for pages that haven't been reviewed or updated for a long time, particularly if they contain information that changes regularly.

Search for years in page titles and URLs.

Check old PDFs, expired event pages, campaign landing pages and staff profiles.

Run broken-link reports.

And pay attention to pages that keep generating questions from students or colleagues — repeated clarification requests are often a clue that something isn't working.

Your analytics can help!

If you have a high-traffic page that hasn't been reviewed in two years, that deserves more attention than an old page nobody visits.

Internal search data can also show you what people are looking for and whether they're being sent to several competing versions of the same answer.

Then there's search itself

Try searching your own institution for some of the information that matters most:

"[Your university] tuition fees"

"[Your university] application deadline"

"[Your university] entry requirements"

"[Your university] scholarships"

"[Your university] accommodation costs"

If an old PDF, expired page or conflicting version is ranking alongside your current information, prospective students can find it too.

Our SEO, AEO and GEO playbook for higher ed goes deeper into why clear, authoritative pages matter across traditional and AI search.

Your CMS/DXP can be a detective!

Your CMS/DXP platform should also be able to help and can take some of the administrative load: content owners, review dates, expiry dates, reminders, scheduled unpublishing, approval workflows and reports highlighting pages that haven't been reviewed recently.

It can't tell you whether a course description is still accurate, of course, somebody still has to make that judgement, but it can make forgotten content much easier to spot.

Depending on your setup, look for:

reports showing old content

pages without an owner

content approaching an expiry date

broken links

sections that haven't been reviewed recently.

Don't underestimate your own teams

Admissions, recruitment, student services and faculty staff often know exactly which pages cause problems because they're the people answering the resulting questions.

A full content audit can be useful, but you don't necessarily need to start with the whole website.

We'd start with the content most closely connected to student decisions, find the weak spots there and work outwards.

Keep it, change it, or get rid of it (a.k.a Kiss, Marry, Kill)

Fun way to figure out what to do with older content?

Some pages simply need updating, but you can maybe comnine others because somehow you've ended up with three pages answering the same question.

An old URL could still attract useful traffic and so you may want to redirect it, while historical material may belong in an archive.

And some pages have simply reached the end of their useful life and you need to do the deed.

Deleting content can make higher ed teams understandably nervous, particularly when nobody knows who might still be linking to it.

That's where redirects, analytics, and a proper content inventory can make the decision considerably less alarming (trust us!).

A little maintenance goes a long way: start this now

Content maintenance doesn't have to mean shutting the doors for a three-month university-wide audit.

You might start with your highest-risk recruitment content.

Review expired campaign pages after every admissions cycle.

Run regular broken-link checks.

Make content reassignment part of the process when somebody leaves.

Look at older PDFs and ask whether they still need to exist at all.

Done regularly, these are fairly small jobs.

Left until a major redesign or migration, they can become very big ones.

And perhaps that's the easiest way to look at outdated content.

Your university or college already puts a huge amount of effort into attracting prospective students and creating better digital journeys.

Keeping the information at the end of those journeys accurate is part of the same job.

title: Enhancing student learning through innovative scholarship
summary: by Jenny Burnham, Matt Mears, Kennedy Offor, Jane Woodin and Tim Herrick This blog is a report on the Enhancing Student Learning Through Innovative Scholarship (ESLTIS) conference held at the University of Sheffield in July 2026. The conference involved participants … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Jenny Burnham, Matt Mears, Kennedy Offor, Jane Woodin and Tim Herrick

This blog is a report on the Enhancing Student Learning Through Innovative Scholarship (ESLTIS) conference held at the University of Sheffield in July 2026. The conference involved participants from 24 different universities and nearly 50 sessions.

When higher education faces real pressure, coming together to reimagine how we teach and learn is more than just professional development – it is a vital act of community. In July 2026, 97 educators, researchers, and student partners gathered at the University of Sheffield for two energising days at the Enhancing Student Learning Through Innovative Scholarship (ESLTIS) conference.

Across two inspiring keynotes, 39 talks and oral bites, and seven hands-on workshops, the atmosphere was filled with practical optimism, bold experimentation, and genuine connection. At a time when financial constraints weigh heavily across the sector, ESLTIS 2026 proved that an exceptional, high-impact academic gathering does not have to cost the earth. By keeping delegate fees as low as possible without compromising on quality, the conference demonstrated that transformative scholarship can remain accessible, inclusive, and deeply rewarding for everyone involved.

To capture the spirit of those two days, this blog brings together the key ideas, personal reflections, and practical insights that defined the event. We explore the overarching themes shaping the sector, followed by firsthand perspectives from our keynote speaker, insights from a session chair navigating AI in the curriculum, and the invaluable contributions of our student partners.

Key Conference Themes

With the tone of ‘Dealing with Disruption’ set by Professor Sam Nolan, the conference explored how learning and teaching in higher education is responding to and being shaped by the outside influences bringing both adversity and opportunity into the sector. A recurrent theme of innovations drawing on AI technology encompassed support for diverse student needs, its use in assessment, and as a teaching aid. The conference mirrored the acknowledgement of the evolving higher education demographic, with discussions covering inclusivity, decolonisation, engagement, identity, and self-worth, with structured gap-filling support, and breaking down of participation barriers, busting out of disciplinary silos to support students’ belonging and wellbeing. Wide-ranging talks covered: curriculum both hidden and carefully designed, strategies to augment students’ development of their skills and their readiness for their post-graduation world, and experiences of collaboration with and between students, staff, and professional services teams

Underpinning it all was the continuing ethos of the ESLTIS community that recognises and celebrates the education-focus of academia, exploring this with talks and workshops on academic identity – how it grows and develops, the things that shape it, and how it can be described and evidenced. The conference was not one thing for all delegates, it had something for everyone; areas with which we are familiar and aspects provoking thought and reflection, from which we could learn. Yet again, I have attended a conference and come away with more than I expected.

Reflections from a keynote speaker

Dr Jenny Burnham is a Senior University Teacher in Chemistry at the University of Sheffield. Here she writes about her career and how she shared her experience at the conference.

I am interested in everything and my career highlights have been similarly eclectic. Rather than focus on a single speciality, I used myself as the common thread to weave a story that would be useful, relevant, or inspirational for a diverse audience of enthusiastic and accomplished educators. Taking inspiration from the conference name and conference themes (academic identity, community in learning and teaching, SoTL, supporting student success, and learning and teaching possibilities), my keynote made a virtue of the meanders of my academic career so far.

My academic journey started in chemistry, shaping my relationship with information (evidence is key) and placing the primacy of experimental investigation at the centre of my disciplinary awareness. My early scholarship interests grew from this, exploring the development of inquiry skills through laboratory education. Spending a lot of time teaching students in the lab and enjoying their individuality shaped a desire to see them all succeed. This developed into an education philosophy that students are clever and capable with enormous potential, which permeates my work. An MEd drawing on what can be learned from sharing practice and insight (Rowland, 1999) transformed my approach to education. The benefits I felt in sharing my work with people who were interested motivated me to extend my networks. These have been a source of inspiration, opportunity and support, and allowed me to define my leadership identity; supporting, facilitating, promoting, and enabling collegial interaction and growth within my community.

My keynote aimed to provide a little of something for everyone, and evidence that I succeeded in this is captured in three different post-keynote interactions. I was thanked for owning my nerves: “it helps” she said. I had lunch with a PhD chemist considering an academic career; and I received an enquiry about a Learning Landscapes initiatives I worked on. There was something for me too: a final, unexpected result of my talk was that pulling it together reminded me of the cool stuff I have done. Celebrating successes is definitely something I intend to do more of.

Reflections from a session chair

Dr Kennedy Offor was a member of the local organising committee and reflects on his experiences at ESLTIS in the role of session chair.

Chairing the ‘AI in the Curriculum’ session gave me with a unique perspective on how colleagues from different disciplines are responding to the rapid emergence of generative AI in higher education. Although the eight presentations ranged from institutional policy to engineering, mathematics, business, humanities, and language learning, a common thread emerged throughout the session – how learning, assessment, and curriculum design should evolve to ensure that students continue to develop critical judgement, disciplinary understanding, and professional responsibility. The discussion reflected a noticeable shift from reacting to AI as a disruptive technology towards designing learning environments that make purposeful and educationally meaningful use of it.

Laurie Wilson opened the session by introducing the University of Sheffield’s developing ‘Common Approach to AI in the Curriculum’, emphasising “harmonisation rather than homogenisation” and arguing that AI should support good disciplinary teaching rather than drive it. Joanne Irving-Walton then offered a thought-provoking perspective by examining the “gaps” where judgement develops, suggesting that AI increasingly participates in the uncertainty, rehearsal and reflection through which students and educators learn.

Panos Kloukinas, Nick McCullen and Will Roberts built on this by arguing that mathematics and computation education should increasingly prioritise application, interpretation and problem formulation over procedural execution, while Dawn Whitton demonstrated how students could critically evaluate AI itself through a staged business assessment that required them not only to use AI, but also to critique its assumptions, biases and wider societal implications.

The engineering perspective was represented through our own presentation, which used longitudinal Graduate Teaching Assistant reflections to show how observations of student uncertainty, teamwork and AI use informed iterative redesign of an MSc engineering design module. Mireilla Bikanga Ada’s graduate study provided an interesting counterpoint by showing that, despite widespread AI adoption, teamwork remained the strongest predictor of graduates’ perceptions of degree relevance.

Rachel Johnson illustrated how a simple, low-stakes classroom activity could encourage students critically to examine AI-generated information and its biases, while Franziska Collier demonstrated how AI avatars could provide authentic, low-risk opportunities for students to practise high-stakes language assessments.

The discussions reinforced my own view that the key educational question is no longer whether students should use AI, but how curricula can help them develop the professional judgement needed to use it responsibly. Rather than diminishing the role of educators, the session demonstrated that AI makes thoughtful curriculum design, assessment, and disciplinary expertise more important than ever, and highlighted an encouraging direction of travel for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning community.

Students as Partners

Dr. Jane Woodin was a member of the local organising committee and offers her thoughts on working with students as volunteer partners

The conference ethos of inclusive dialogue was also evident in the organisation of student volunteers who were invited to participate in whatever they wished, from visiting and advising on the venue beforehand, supporting registration and general enquiries, and co-chairing sessions together with a staff volunteer. Responses from the eight volunteers ranged from tentative interest in helping out to requests to ‘have a go at everything’, and others who did the minimum in terms of active volunteering because they found the topics of the talk so interesting and important.

It was heartening to hear one volunteer offer to sit at the front of the large auditorium to oversee a presentation session, handling the Q &A masterfully, including interventions from the co-chair. Another volunteer started out shyly offering to help at the registration desk, but seeing fellow students taking the chairing role, threw herself into it enthusiastically.

These experiences remind us how the processes surrounding education are as important as the education itself – or perhaps are or should be inseparable, as the ‘way that you do it’ melds seamlessly into ‘what you do’; offering an example of SoTL in action at its best.

Final Reflections

Dr Matt Mears is a Senior University Teacher in Physics at the University of Sheffield, and was chair of the Local Organising Committee for ESLTIS2026

As Conference Chair, reflecting on the energy across those two days fills me with immense pride and a distinct sense of gratitude. While hosting an event of this scale undoubtedly takes work, the dividend it pays back to the host team and the wider community is extraordinary. Watching colleagues reconnect, draw genuine inspiration from such a rich variety of presenters, and spark new collaborations in real time reminded me why these gatherings are so vital for our sector.

If you have ever toyed with the idea of organising a conference, or perhaps bringing ESLTIS to your own institution, I cannot encourage you enough to take the leap. The effort involved is far outweighed by the connection, camaraderie, and fresh momentum it generates. Whether as an attender, a presenter, or a future host, I look forward to seeing where our community goes next.

Dr Jenny Burnham is a chemistry university teaching specialist with 20 years’ experience teaching and learning about education at the University of Sheffield.

Dr Matt Mears is a Senior University Teacher in Physics in the School of Mathematical and Physical Sciences at the University of Sheffield. His research focuses on inclusive education practices and laboratory-based teaching.

Dr Kennedy Offor is an engineering educator and researcher with experience teaching undergraduate and postgraduate engineering at the University of Sheffield’s School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering and, more recently, apprenticeship and technical engineering education at the AMRC Training Centre.

Dr. Jane Woodin is a Senior University Teacher in the School of Languages, Arts and Societies at the University of Sheffield. She has taught and researched in intercultural communication, focusing on peer interaction and dialogue approaches.

Dr Tim Herrick is a Senior University Teacher in the School of Education, and a National Teaching Fellow. He was part of the ESLTIS conference committee and helped co-ordinate this blogpost.
